name.text: Accounting for Variability: accounting for journey time

questiontext.text:
A traveller is catching a long-distance bus to Kisumu, which leaves from the city centre. How many minutes should they allow to get there?

With no information at all, the typical trip into town takes 60 minutes. Six clue cards each tell you something about this particular trip. Two cards are free; you can turn over more, but each extra card costs some marks.

How to play

  1. Turn over cards by clicking them. Two are free. Each extra card takes 10% off your marks for Step 3, and cards can't be turned back.
  2. Work out your prediction with the charts below: start at 60 minutes and add the adjustment for each card you turned over.
  3. Decide how many minutes to allow. Any cards still face down, and plain chance, can still change the trip, so you may want some spare time.
  4. Press Check. All six cards and the actual journey time are then revealed.

Scoring. Reaching the bus with anything from 0 to 60 minutes to spare is a good result. More than 60 minutes is a long wait, so it gets half marks. Arriving after the time you allowed means a missed bus and no marks.

What a local driver knows

Day and time of day. Each cell shows how much that day and time adds to or takes off the typical 60 minutes.

  • If you turned over both the Day and Time of day cards, use the cell where they meet.
  • If you turned over only one of them, use its average at the edge of the chart.

For example, if you know it is a Friday at 17:30, add +35. If you only know it is a Friday, add the Friday average of +8.

generalfeedback.text:
The cards that can move the trip most are day and time of day (together, from 20 minutes quicker to 35 minutes slower) and traffic news (a 20-minute swing between no incidents and an incident). Pickup point and weather come next. Driver rating never changes the trip, so turning it over accounts for none of the variation.

The heatmap's edges show what you can account for with only one of the day or time cards. Friday's average is +8, but a Friday evening is much worse than a Friday morning. Knowing both cards accounts for more.

Any cards left face down are real, known causes, but your prediction leaves them out: that is unaccounted-for variability. The final few minutes either way are natural variability, which no card could predict. A sensible allowance is your prediction plus some spare time. You can do well with two cards and a good buffer, without paying for more.

Your cards accounted for {@accS@} minutes. The rest of the clues added {@unaccS@} minutes. Those are real, known causes of delay, but they weren't in your prediction because those cards were face down. That is what unaccounted-for variability means: it isn't random, it just hasn't been included. The last {@noiseS@} minutes were natural variability: even with every card turned over, no one could have predicted them.
